Withdrawal means the act of pulling something back, taking something away, or stepping away from something. Think of it like a hand reaching into a space and then pulling back out. That pulling-back motion — that is the essence of withdrawal.

The word is used in many different situations in everyday life, but this single core idea runs through all of them.

1. Taking Money Out of a Bank

This is probably the most common, everyday use of the word.

When you go to a bank or ATM and take your own money out of your account, that act is called a withdrawal.

"She made a withdrawal of ₹5,000 from her savings account."

The opposite of this is a deposit (putting money in). So withdrawal = money coming out; deposit = money going in.

2. Removing or Taking Back Something (Formally or Officially)

Withdrawal can refer to officially taking something back or cancelling something that was offered, stated, or given.

Examples:

  • A company might announce the withdrawal of a product from the market — meaning they are removing it and it will no longer be available.
  • A lawyer might file for the withdrawal of a legal case — meaning they are pulling the case back and dropping it.
  • A person might make the withdrawal of a statement — meaning they are taking back something they said, declaring it no longer stands.
  • A job offer can be withdrawn — meaning the company cancels the offer before you have accepted it.

The key idea here: something that was present, available, or in circulation is now being pulled back.

3. The Retreat of Soldiers or Forces (Military)

In a military context, withdrawal means pulling troops or forces back from a position, region, or conflict. It is a retreat — but "withdrawal" sounds more planned and deliberate than just running away.

"The army began its withdrawal from the northern border."
"The country negotiated a full withdrawal of foreign troops from its territory."

4. Stepping Back from People or Situations (Emotional/Social)

A person can also withdraw from the world around them. When someone pulls back emotionally, stops engaging, avoids others, or becomes quiet and distant, this is called withdrawal.

"After the loss of his father, he retreated into a state of withdrawal, rarely speaking to anyone."
"Her therapist noticed a gradual withdrawal from her social life."

This kind of withdrawal can be a natural coping response to pain, stress, or trauma — or it can be a sign of depression or anxiety. The person is not physically leaving, but emotionally and socially, they are pulling back.

5. Stopping a Substance — Drug or Alcohol Withdrawal

This is one of the most medically important uses of the word. When a person has been regularly using a drug (such as heroin, alcohol, nicotine, sleeping pills, or even strong pain medications), their body becomes physically dependent on that substance. The body adjusts itself around the constant presence of the drug.

When the person suddenly stops using the substance, the body goes into a kind of shock — it doesn't know how to function without what it had come to rely on. The collection of physical and mental symptoms that result from this stopping is called withdrawal (or drug withdrawal / alcohol withdrawal).

Common withdrawal symptoms can include:

  • Sweating and shaking
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Anxiety and irritability
  • Insomnia (inability to sleep)
  • Intense cravings for the substance
  • In severe cases (especially with alcohol), seizures or even death

"The patient was going through alcohol withdrawal and had to be monitored closely by doctors."

The phrase "withdrawal symptoms" is very commonly used — it refers to these specific reactions the body has when a drug it depended on is suddenly removed.

Note: Withdrawal in this medical sense is not a sign of moral weakness — it is a physical phenomenon, a biological reaction of the body.

6. Pulling Back an Application or Request

When someone has formally submitted something — a job application, a university application, a proposal, a bid — and they then cancel or take it back before a decision is made, this is called a withdrawal.

"He submitted his withdrawal from the competition two days before the event."
"The candidate announced her withdrawal from the election."

Across all these uses, notice that withdrawal always involves something being present and then being pulled away — whether it is:

  • money (from a bank),
  • troops (from a region),
  • a person (from social life),
  • a drug (from the body),
  • a statement or application (from the table).

The direction is always the same: outward, away, back.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Removal is more about taking something out permanently, often by force or authority. Withdrawal has more of a sense of pulling back voluntarily or deliberately.
  • Retreat is specifically about moving away from a threat, often used in military contexts. Withdrawal can be planned and strategic, and is broader — it applies to many non-military situations.
  • Abstinence means choosing not to use something (e.g., alcohol) in the first place. Withdrawal happens specifically after a period of regular use, when you stop.

"Withdrawal" is a fairly formal and serious word. You wouldn't say "I went to the ATM for a withdrawal" in casual conversation — you'd more likely say "I took out some cash." But in writing, official documents, medical contexts, and news reporting, withdrawal is the precise and appropriate word to use.
